newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Oil and gas outlook bright in 1997 - analysts. [CORRECTED 07:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Oil and gas outlook bright in 1997 - analysts. [CORRECTED 07:00 GMT]

text.p: Australia's oil and gas sector is poised to shine brighter this year, analysts say, driven by a 1996 surge in exploration and corporate activity.

The energy index rose 49 percent (corrects from 82 percent) last year, underpinned by strong oil prices, compared with a rise of about 10 percent (corrects from 27 percent) in the overall share market's All Ordinaries Index.
"The sector will still do well, even though everybody anticipates that oil prices will come off or show some volatility," said Macquarie Equities Ltd analyst Peter Best.

Exploration hotspots include the Timor Gap (shared between Australia and Indonesia), where major oil companies Woodside Petroleum Ltd and Santos Ltd plan to drill key wells, and where the Laminaria and Elang oil fields are set for development.
In Papua New Guinea, Oil Search Ltd has received development licences for the Gobe oil field and continues to appraise the promising Moran field.
Planning continues on a potential pipeline to take gas from PNG to Queensland, with the Pandora gas field partners combining their expertise with Kutubu operator Chevron Corp.
Best said the Carnarvon Basin off Western Australia would be a focus for both gas contracts and exploration, with newly listed Tap Oil NL and Santos the main players.
The area remained under-explored following a pullback by some of the majors and had potential for finds in the 25-50 million barrels of oil range.
More takeovers are expected following successful bids for Ampolex Ltd, Discovery Petroleum NL and Command Petroleum Holdings NL during 1996.
"There's no question that you will see continuing corporate activity," says James Capel Australia Ltd oil and gas analyst Mario Traviati.
"Oil companies have strong oil prices, their cash flows are very strong, they've got a lot of money in the bank," he said.
Producers could either put their money into exploration, with its long lead-times, or buy production. "If there's value at the corporate level, companies will chase that first."
Petroz NL, Cultus Petroleum NL, Novus Petroleum Ltd and Tap Oil, were at the quality end of second line companies, Traviati said.
"They would be the ones that would be attracting the biggest (takeover) interest," he said.

Shaw Stockbroking Ltd analyst John Colnan said overseas buyers would look for higher quality long-term assets, such as companies already producing oil and gas or those with very good exploration acreage.
Buyers also preferred simple companies with a major asset, such as Command's Ravva field in India and Discovery's Kakap field in Indonesia.

Several brokers nominated Petroz NL as a potential target, given its 14.95 percent interest in the Undan permit, part of the Bayu-Undan oil field in the Timor Gap where a further development decision is expected around April.
Petroz's share price has risen from around 67 cents in mid-September to more than 90 cents.
Colnan said the performance for the overall index would depend on the oil price, and the severity of the Northern Hemisphere winter.
A harsh winter could spark a jump in the oil price to US$30, for an average over 1997 of US$25 a barrel, he said.
"If that's the case, I think there's another 10 or 20 percent in the sector."
Any fall in the oil price would affect the majors, rather than smaller companies that were focussing on exploration, said Traviati.
"People aren't really buying them for earnings, they are buying them for a roll of the dice and some high potential exploration."
Traviati said Woodside and Santos appeared fully priced, although Best expected both companies to book fairly big reserves for the 1996 year.
Best noted that some of the second-line companies were being supported by the smaller number available for investors to choose from. "There is the same amount of money and fewer companies," he said.
This could lead to the float of new companies, around the size of Tap's A$46 million float in September.
Best said the overall sector should also be boosted by the prospects for gas projects, such as Bayu Undan and those in PNG.
"A lot of people are fairly sceptical about these various projects going ahead," he said.
"But with deregulation, more infrastructure and the switch to gas-fired power stations there will be increasing momentum."
--Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1871
